passage: Mentor's note, Kiran. Tushar was quiet at Thursday's check-in and, when I asked, said he had watched the shift lead sign the weekly stock-count sheet without walking the shelves. "It is probably fine," he said twice, and looked at the table. He said it was not his place and that he feared being labelled a complainer in his first year. I did not tell him what to do. I asked what question he could ask that would be true and not an accusation. He came up with, "Did I miss when the shelf count was done?" I noted that he sounded relieved to say it aloud. We agreed he would try it on Monday and tell me how it went.

qa.q: How many times did Tushar say "It is probably fine"?
qa.a: Tushar said it twice.

qa.q: What was Tushar afraid of?
qa.a: Being labelled a complainer in his first year, and he was unsure whether it was his place.

qa.q: What question did Tushar come up with, and why is it a good approach?
qa.a: He came up with "Did I miss when the shelf count was done?", which is true and not an accusation.

qa.q: How might the shift lead react to a calm question about the count?
qa.a: Perhaps caught off guard, but the question leaves room to answer without being accused, and it could prompt the count to be done.

grounding: Illustrates a coworker who sees a questionable practice, doubts whether it is their business and fears the cost of speaking up.

Tuesday, 11:50 p.m. Saw it again today. Sahil filled in his site-visit sheet for the whole week and put down two visits on days he was in the office; I know because I sat next to him. It is not my job to police anyone, is it? And what if I have the dates wrong? Sahil is well liked and I am still on probation. So I made tea, said nothing and sat with my laptop feeling small. It has been three weeks. Riya from accounts asked whether the sheets looked normal and I said, "Seems so." I am writing this down because I wish I had simply asked, "Hey, did I get the dates wrong for those two sites?" Maybe tomorrow. Maybe.
Dhruv

qa.q: How many site visits did Dhruv notice on Sahil's sheet that did not match?
qa.a: Dhruv noticed two visits on days Sahil was in the office.

qa.q: What is Dhruv worried about?
qa.a: Being wrong about the dates and the cost of speaking up while still on probation, so Dhruv feels small and uneasy.

qa.q: What could Dhruv say to Sahil?
qa.a: Ask, "Did I get the dates wrong for those two sites?" as a question and not an accusation.

qa.q: How might Sahil react to that question?
qa.a: Perhaps surprised, then check the dates and correct them, or feel defensive; the question leaves a way to answer without an accusation.

grounding: Illustrates a coworker who notices a questionable practice, stays silent from doubt and fear, and wishes to have asked a question.

In the block office in Chhindwara, Zainab had been a data clerk for eight months. Her job was to enter the rural job scheme attendance into the computer.
One afternoon, she noticed Jagdish sir, the senior clerk, filling in the muster roll for Dhanora village. He was marking twelve names present for days when, she knew, the work had stopped because of rain. She had seen the photos from the site.
He saw her looking. "Arre, they'll work double next week. It balances out."
Zainab said nothing. She typed the numbers as they were written. It wasn't her village, not her roll. She was new. He had helped her get the job.
Three months later, a social audit team came to Dhanora. The villagers said they had not been paid for the rainy weeks at all; the wages had gone to other names. Jagdish sir was suspended.
Zainab sat at her desk that day, thinking of the question she hadn't asked.

qa.q: How many names did Jagdish sir mark present?
qa.a: He was marking twelve names present.

qa.q: Why did Zainab say nothing when she saw the roll?
qa.a: Zainab was afraid and unsure, being new and owing Jagdish sir for helping her get the job.

qa.q: What small step could Zainab have taken?
qa.a: Zainab could have asked Jagdish sir, or the block officer, about the rainy days, or noted what she saw with the date.

qa.q: How did Jagdish sir seem to see his own marking at the time?
qa.a: Jagdish sir treated it as harmless balancing, saying they would work double next week, without facing that wages could go to the wrong people.

grounding: An observer clerk sees a senior falsify attendance, stays silent out of fear and uncertainty, and later wishes she had asked a question.

In the restaurant kitchen in Berlin, Chidi was on the early prep shift. At 7 a.m., he saw Elif, the sous chef, peel the date labels off three trays of chicken and stick on new ones with today's date.
He knew those trays had come in on Monday. It was Thursday.
Elif had given him this job. She had covered for him the time he was late. He told himself maybe she knew something he didn't. He went on chopping onions, but his hands felt stiff all morning.
At 4 p.m., as service drew near, he couldn't stand it. He found her by the cold room and asked quietly, "Elif, are these the Monday trays?"
She stopped. Then she sighed. "Yes. I didn't want to waste them."
"I don't think we can serve them."
After a long moment, she nodded, and they put the trays in the waste bin together. She told the head chef herself.
Later, Chidi wished he had asked at seven, not four.

qa.q: On which day had the trays come in?
qa.a: Those trays had come in on Monday.

qa.q: How did Chidi feel after seeing the labels changed?
qa.a: Chidi felt uneasy and afraid to speak, his hands stiff all morning, torn by loyalty to Elif.

qa.q: What did Chidi do that protected the diners, and what would have been better?
qa.a: He asked Elif a quiet question before service and they binned the trays; asking at seven, right away, would have been better still.

qa.q: How might Elif have felt when Chidi asked his question?
qa.a: Elif probably felt caught and a little ashamed, then relieved enough to agree and tell the head chef herself.

grounding: An observer colleague sees food relabelled, stays silent for hours out of fear, then asks a question that protects diners, wishing he had asked sooner.

passage:
In the college admissions office, Nitin was sorting forms when he saw Jahnavi, the senior clerk, pull one file from the waiting-list tray and slip it into the "admitted" pile. The surname on it matched hers. She caught him looking and smiled. "Paperwork backlog," she said.
Nitin turned back to his screen. The waiting list had been published that morning. The file she'd moved was number forty-two on it. Numbers one to forty-one were still waiting.
He thought about asking, "Did the committee approve this one?" He even opened his mouth. Then he pictured the office afterwards, her cold face every morning, his contract ending in March.
He said nothing. At lunch he ate quickly and didn't join the others.
A week later, a girl who had been number six on the list came to the counter asking why nobody had called. Nitin handed her a token and wished, very badly, that he had asked his question.

qa.q: What number was the moved file on the waiting list?
qa.a: Number forty-two.

qa.q: Why did Nitin stay silent?
qa.a: Nitin was afraid of what asking would cost, picturing Jahnavi's cold face every morning and his contract ending in March.

qa.q: What simple question could Nitin have asked, and why might it help?
qa.a: "Did the committee approve this one?" is a question rather than an accusation, and could have brought the move into the open while the list was fresh.

qa.q: What is it like for the girl who was number six?
qa.a: She is left confused and waiting, asking why nobody called while a file lower on the list was moved ahead.

grounding: Shows a coworker seeing a questionable practice, staying silent out of fear, and later wishing they had asked a question.
